requirements.description: Poor performance alone is NOT a listed s.78 termination ground; it can only lead to termination indirectly, via becoming an excludable-supplier

essential_evidence.verification_note: CORRECTED (this was the specific issue the audit brief flagged): verified s.78's full text via legislation.gov.uk. s.78's implied termination term applies ONLY where a 'termination ground' is met: (i) the contract was awarded/modified in material breach of the Act, (ii) the supplier became an excluded or excludable supplier after award, or (iii) a sub-contractor is excluded/excludable. Poor performance ON ITS OWN is NOT one of these grounds. The real chain is: repeated poor performance after a proper opportunity to improve (s.71(4)) triggers a PUBLICATION duty (s.71(5)) - it does not by itself terminate anything. Separately, if that same poor performance is serious enough to meet a Schedule 7 paragraph 12 discretionary exclusion ground (breach of a relevant contract, sufficiently serious), the supplier could become 'excludable', which WOULD then satisfy s.78's termination ground (ii). So the answer to 'can we terminate for poor performance on its own' is NO, not directly - termination requires the additional step of the poor performance also meeting the higher bar of an exclusion ground, which is not automatic.
Confirmed chunk_ids UKSI_2015_102__UKSI_2015_102__SEG_0073__CH_001/002, PCR2015. Three mandatory grounds, none general poor-performance.

Added: this is the actual discretionary exclusion ground ('breach of a relevant contract... sufficiently serious') that repeated poor performance would need to satisfy for the supplier to become 'excludable' and thereby trigger s.78's termination ground - without this step, s.78 alone does not authorise termination for poor performance. Confirmed present in the corpus at chunk_id UKPGA_2023_54__NODEV1__CH_00279 (independently confirmed by direct SQL query this session).

requirements.description: VERIFIED: Schedule 5 direct-award justifications are a route for awarding a contract without competition directly (not via a framework). A call-off under a framework without further competition is instead governed by s.45(4), which permits award without competition where the framework has only one supplier, or where it fixes the core contract terms and provides an objective supplier-selection mechanism.

PLAUSIBLE, PARTIALLY VERIFIED: s.45(4) requires an 'objective mechanism for supplier selection' but the Act text as fetched does not itself state whether unfettered discretion to pick any provider satisfies 'objective' — this is an interpretive/practitioner-risk question, not one the statute answers explicitly.
Section 49 ties the 4-year single-supplier framework limit to the point at which a lot has only one supplier appointed, applied independently per lot.

Section 49(2) requires at least three separate framework awards within an open framework scheme (an award within year 3, and a further award within each subsequent 5-year period) — a single second framework cannot simply be run to the full 8-year limit in place of a required third award.
Call-off contracts may extend beyond the life of the framework itself where a longer duration is reasonably justified for that specific contract.

Section 49(4) permits an authority, where supplier numbers under an open framework are unlimited, to reappoint an existing supplier by reference to its prior appointment or an earlier/current tender, without requiring a fresh submission — though the authority may alternatively choose to require one.
A tender notice must be published for a Dynamic Market call-off, restricted to Dynamic Market members, while allowing outside suppliers to apply for admission to the market beforehand.
